Appenzell
ap'en-tsel
n. (Swiss canton divided in 1597 into Reformed Outer Rhodes and Catholic Inner Rhodes)
From Latin abbatis cella, the abbot's cell, of the abbey of St Gallen; German Appenzell.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

Appenzell is the one Swiss canton that solved its religious division by dividing itself. Reformed preaching took the outer, weaving parishes while the inner, pastoral valleys held to Rome, and after seventy years of quarrels over the mass, the monasteries and the pulpits, the canton split in 1597 into Ausserrhoden, Reformed, and Innerrhoden, Catholic, each with its own assembly, each keeping the name. The settlement kept the peace for three centuries and is still on the map. The dictionary records Appenzell because the case is genuinely hard and the lesson is double-edged: a formal separation can be the honest end of an irreconcilable difference, and it can also be the institutionalising of a wound. Scripture does not applaud division — “that there be no divisions among you” (1Co 1:10) — yet it also requires separation where doctrine is at stake, and commands the church to “mark them which cause divisions and offences contrary to the doctrine which ye have learned; and avoid them” (Rom 16:17). Appenzell is where both sentences had to be held at once.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines schism as a division or separation in church affairs and a breach of unity, division as the act of dividing or a part separated from the rest, and concord as union in opinions and interests.

expand to see more

SCHISM, n. In church affairs, a division or separation; a breach of unity among people of the same religious faith.

DIVISION, n. The act of dividing; a part separated from the rest; a portion; a section.

CON'CORD, n. Agreement between persons; union in opinions, sentiments, views or interests.

PEACE, n. In a general sense, a state of quiet or tranquillity; freedom from disturbance or agitation.

Key Scripture

1Co 1:10 — "Now I beseech you, brethren, by the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, that ye all speak the same thing, and that there be no divisions among you; but that ye be perfectly joined together in the same mind and in the same judgment."

Rom 16:17 — "Now I beseech you, brethren, mark them which cause divisions and offences contrary to the doctrine which ye have learned; and avoid them."

Mat 12:25 — "And Jesus knew their thoughts, and said unto them, Every kingdom divided against itself is brought to desolation; and every city or house divided against itself shall not stand:"

Eph 4:3 — "Endeavouring to keep the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace."

Modern Corruption

The canton that divided itself in 1597, Reformed Outer Rhodes and Catholic Inner Rhodes, and kept the peace for three centuries.

expand to see more

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The live misuse runs in both directions. One error calls every separation sinful and so keeps contradictory doctrines yoked together in one body until neither is taught. The other treats separation as costless, so that a congregation divides over preference and calls it conscience.

The principle to recover is that unity is commanded and so is doctrinal separation, and the two are reconciled only by the word. The command is plain: “that ye all speak the same thing, and that there be no divisions among you” (1Co 1:10), and the church is to be “Endeavouring to keep the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace” (Eph 4:3). But the ground of separation is equally plain, and it is doctrine: “mark them which cause divisions and offences contrary to the doctrine which ye have learned; and avoid them” (Rom 16:17). The warning against a house at war with itself stands over both parties: “every city or house divided against itself shall not stand” (Mat 12:25).

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Greek schisma (G4978), a rent or division; Greek henotes (G1775), unity.

expand to see more

Greek schisma (G4978) — a rent, a tear, a division in a body; 1 Corinthians 1:10.

Greek dichostasia (G1370) — a standing apart, dissension; Romans 16:17.

Greek skandalon (G4625) — a stumbling-block, an offence; Romans 16:17.

Greek henotes (G1775) — oneness, unity to be kept; Ephesians 4:3.

Greek eirene (G1515) — peace, the bond in which unity is kept; Ephesians 4:3.

Usage

"“that there be no divisions among you” (1Co 1:10) — seventy years of quarrel over the mass and the pulpits."

"“mark them which cause divisions and offences contrary to the doctrine” (Rom 16:17) — the division of 1597 into Outer and Inner Rhodes."

"“Endeavouring to keep the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace” (Eph 4:3) — three centuries of peace on a divided map."
